previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis, hepatitis C, bladder and prostate cancer s/p ileal conduit, and chronic anemia presented after a fall due to lightheadedness and weakness. He had a recent episode of stoma bleeding sutured in the ED and was found to have acute on chronic blood loss anemia, requiring one unit of packed red blood cells. His fall was attributed to alcohol intoxication (ETOH 96), possible orthostasis, and anemia. He exhibited transient left facial droop and weakness, prompting neurology consultation and recommendation for non-urgent MRI to rule out stroke. Toxic encephalopathy was suspected due to alcohol use, though he remained alert. Urinalysis revealed pyuria with a positive culture for Klebsiella pneumoniae, though antibiotics were withheld due to absence of systemic infection. Abdominal ultrasound showed patent hepatic vasculature with reversed flow in the left portal vein, no ascites, and mild left hydronephrosis. The patient became agitated, refused further testing, and left against medical advice after stabilization. He was advised to follow up with neurology, urology, and hepatology.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___, 

It was a pleasure to take care of you at ___. You were 
admitted for a urinary tract infection affecting your surgical 
bladder. The bacteria causing the infection are strong and 
resistant to most antibiotics, so you required strong 
antibiotics through the IV. You completed a full 10 day course 
of Linezolid and Cefipime.

While you were here, you developed a problem with bleeding. 
First you were bleeding from your gut. We think this is because 
your platelets (a part of your blood that stops bleeding) were 
very low, and because of your liver disease. Later, you 
developed bleeding from your stoma. You needed several 
transfusions, because your blood counts were low. You were 
transferred to the intensive care unit, where they made a new 
path for blood to flow from your gut back to your heart without 
passing through your liver, lowering the pressure in your 
vessels, and a procedure to scar down the bleeding vessels 
themselves. After this your bleeding resolved.

You also developed some confusion while you were here. We think 
this is because you liver is not able to clear toxins from your 
blood as effectively anymore. For this confusion, it is very 
important that you continue to take lactulose and rifaximin.

Unfortunately, you left the hospital premises before you could 
be safely discharged and given any of this information. We 
called you and asked you to come back to the hospital but you 
refused. We re-inforced the need for you to seek medical care. 
You then hung-up the phone on us. 

We wish you all the best going forward. 

Sincerely,

Your medical team at ___

PROCEDURE:
1. Single lumen PICC placement through the brachial vein on the right.
2. Right axillary venogram.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Using sterile technique and local anesthesia, the brachial
vein on the right was punctured under direct ultrasound guidance using a
micropuncture set. Permanent ultrasound images were obtained before and after
intravenous access, which confirmed vein patency. A peel-away sheath was then
placed over a guidewire.  The guidewire would not advance centrally.  The
peel-away sheath was exchanged for a 4 ___ MPA catheter, which was advanced
into the axillary vein.  The wire was removed and a contrast injection was
performed to perform a right axillary venogram.  The wire was then carefully
directed over the catheter into the right atrium.  The catheter was then
exchanged for the peel-away sheath.  A single lumen PICC measuring 36 cm in
length was then placed through the peel-away sheath with its tip positioned in
the distal SVC under fluoroscopic guidance. Position of the catheter was
confirmed by a fluoroscopic spot film of the chest. The peel-away sheath and
guidewire were then removed. The catheter was secured to the skin, flushed,
and a sterile dressing applied.
The patient tolerated the procedure well. There were no immediate
complications.

3.  Brachialvein approach single lumen right PICC with tip in the distal SVC.

PROCEDURE:  1. Transhepatic portal venous access using ultrasound.
2.  Ultrasound-guided paracentesis.
3.  SMV venogram
4.  Selective right colic venogram.
4.  Sclerosis of stomal varices with alcohol.
5.  Embolization of right colic vein branch (Amplatzer plug).
6.  Post embolization SMV venogram.
7. Right portal vein and IVC pressure measurements.
8.  Right internal jugular venous access.
9. Placement of a 10 mm x 6 cm x 2 cm Viatorr covered stent.
10. Post-stenting balloon angioplasty of the TIPS shunt with a 10 mm balloon.
11. Post-stenting portal venogram.
12.  Post stenting splenic vein and right atrial pressure measurements.
13.  Gel-Foam embolization of the transhepatic access site.


PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
patient. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed
supine on the exam table. A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___
protocol. The neck and right upper abdomen were prepped and draped in the
usual sterile fashion.

Under continuous ultrasound guidance, a branch of the right portal vein was
accessed using a Cook needle.  Upon blood return, a Nitinol wire was passed
into the main portal vein.  A small incision was made at the needle entry
site.  The needle was exchanged for an Accustick set and advanced into the
main portal vein.  The inner stiffener was removed.  A contrast injection
confirmed portal venous anatomy.  Then, a 5 ___ catheter was inserted
into the perihepatic ascitic fluid under direct ultrasound guidance.

An SMV and selective right colic venogram was then performed, with findings
discussed below.  Subsequently, a Glidewire and angled Glidecath were used to
select the enlarged right colic branch feeding the stomal varices.  The
Glidewire was exchanged for an Amplatz wire.  The glide cath was removed, and
___ balloon was advanced and inflated in the distal branch just before
the stomal varices.  Then, 4 cc of alcohol was gently instilled into the
stomal varices.  After 5 minutes, the balloon was deflated.  Then, the 5
___ sheath was exchanged for a 6 ___ sheath, and a 10 mm Amplatzer II
plug was placed in the distal right colic vein branch proximal to the stomal
varices.  A post intervention venogram was performed, with findings discussed
below.  Pressure measurements of the portal vein and IVC were taken.

Given the visualization of rectal varices and elevated portosystemic gradient
of 14, the decision was then made to place a TIPS. Under continuous ultrasound
guidance, the patent right internal jugular vein was compressible and accessed
using a micropuncture needle.  Images of ultrasound access were stored on
PACS. Subsequently a Nitinol wire was passed into the right atrium using
fluoroscopic guidance. A small incision was made at the needle entry site. The
needle was exchanged for a micropuncture sheath. The Nitinol wire was removed
and and Amplatz wire was advanced distally into the IVC.

The micropuncture sheath was then removed and a 10 ___ sheath was advanced
over the wire into the inferior vena cava.  ___ wire and a SOS,
access was obtained in the right hepatic vein. Appropriate position was
confirmed with contrast injection and fluoroscopy in AP and lateral views.

Following procedural planning, the dilator was advanced through the sheath.
Once the sheath was placed in an appropriate position, the cannula device was
inserted over the ___ wire and the wire was exchanged for ___
needle. The angled sheath was turned anteriorly. The needle was then advanced
through liver parenchyma and the needle was withdrawn over its sheath. The
TIPS sheath was withdrawn while gentle suction was applied. Upon blood return,
a Glidewire was introduced into the catheter to pass into the portal vein.  A
straight flush catheter was advanced over the wire and a contrast enhanced
portal venogram was performed. An Amplatz wire was advanced through the
straight flush catheter into the superior mesenteric vein. The catheter was
removed and a 10 mm x 6 cm x 2 cm Viatorr covered covered stent was advanced
into appropriate position and deployed. Following stent deployment, the stent
was dilated using a 10 mm balloon.

The straight flush catheter was advanced over the wire and the wire was
removed.  Proximal splenic vein and right atrial pressure measurements were
performed.  A portal venogram was also performed.

The sheath was then removed from the right internal jugular vein site and
pressure held for 10 minutes to achieve hemostasis. Sterile dressings were
applied.

Gel-Foam torpedoes were placed through the transhepatic access sheath and
deployed.  Then, the transhepatic access sheath was removed, and pressure was
held for 5 minutes to achieve hemostasis.  The ___ catheter was also removed.
Sterile dressings were applied to both of these sites.

The patient tolerated the procedure well.  There were no immediate
post-procedure complications. The patient was transferred to the ICU in stable
condition.

FINDINGS: 

1.  SMV and right colic venogram demonstrates an enlarged right colic vein
feeding a large nest of varices.
2.  Post intervention venogram demonstrates no filling of the stomal varices. 
Rectal varices are noted.
3.  Pre-TIPS portal vein pressure of 27 mm Hg and IVC pressure of 13 mm Hg,
with a portosystemic gradient of 14 mm Hg.
4.  Post-TIPS portal venogram demonstrates brisk flow through the TIPS with
opacification of an anterior abdominal wall varix.
5. Post-TIPS right atrial pressure of 19 and portal pressure of 28 resulting
in portosystemic gradient of 9 mmHg.
6.  1 liter of blood tinged fluid removed through the paracentesis drain.

IMPRESSION: 

1.  Occlusion of stomal varices with alcohol sclerosis and Amplatzer plug
placement.
2. Successful right internal jugular access with transjugular intrahepatic
portosystemic shunt placement with decrease in porto-systemic pressure
gradient.
3.  1 L of blood tinged ascites was drained.
